title: Крёстный отец кухни  (The Godfather of the Kitchen)

segments.t: Continuing his takeover of Arcobaleno's kitchen, Viktor snaps a photo that looks compromising for sous-chef Misha, only for his plan to backfire when Misha's wife walks in. Let's hear the dialogue in Russian first.
Голодаем, значит.
Я там в жульен один новый ингредиент добавил.
Может, посмотрите?
Давайте.
Если ты не хочешь, чтобы это увидела твоя жена,
просто будь доброжелателен ко мне.
Да, шеф, вы прямо крёстный отец.
Всех за ниточки дёргаете.
Что такое? Почему сидим?
Что, нет работы? Всё, уже иду.
Я так, на минутку уходил.
Крёстного отца мамка домой загнала.
Now let's walk through the Russian dialogue together.
Голодаем, значит.
'So we are starving, then.' Chef Barinov centers this short reply on 'to starving', letting a few direct words carry the whole meaning.
Я там в жульен один новый ингредиент добавил.
'I added one new ingredient to the julienne over there.' The past-tense verb ending marks the grammatical gender and number of the subject directly.
Может, посмотрите?
'Maybe you will take a look?' Chef Viktor raises the pitch on the key word to turn this short Russian clause into a direct question.
Давайте.
'Let's see it.' Starting with the everyday word for 'let us' is how Russian speakers warmly invite someone to do something together.
Если ты не хочешь, чтобы это увидела твоя жена,
'If you do not want your wife to see this,' The past-tense verb ending marks the grammatical gender and number of the subject directly.
просто будь доброжелателен ко мне.
'simply be friendly and kind to me.' In everyday Russian, 'simply, just' flows straight into 'kind' without extra linking words.
Да, шеф, вы прямо крёстный отец.
'Yes, Chef, you are regular godfather.' Elena uses the polite plural form of address to maintain a respectful or ironic distance.
Всех за ниточки дёргаете.
'You are pulling everyone's strings.' Notice how Russian puts 'strings' and 'to strings' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
Что такое? Почему сидим?
'What is going on? Why are we sitting around?' Here Elena anchors the thought on 'why' and finishes on 'we are sitting', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
Что, нет работы? Всё, уже иду.
'Is there no work? Alright, I am coming.' In everyday Russian, 'job, work' flows straight into 'am going' without extra linking words.
Я так, на минутку уходил.
'I just stepped away for a minute.' Elena uses the first-person pronoun in the case required by the Russian verb or preposition.
Крёстного отца мамка домой загнала.

'Mommy chased the godfather back home.' Notice how Russian puts 'god-' and 'to home' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect. Let's hear the entire conversation one more time from start to finish.

That covers Viktor blackmailing Misha into obedience right before Misha's wife drags him home. Pay attention to how Russian imperatives form polite requests. See you next time!
До свидания!
